titre: The lake as microcosm (Forbes, 1887): an equilibrium, and lakes that oscillate
accroche: In 1887, an Illinois entomologist describes a small lake as a closed, stable world. The same paper describes lakes that oscillate.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 25, 1887, before the Peoria Scientific Association (Illinois), Stephen A. Forbes reads a paper titled “The Lake as a Microcosm.” He is then Illinois State Entomologist and a professor of zoology. His starting point: a species cannot be understood by studying it alone. To know the black bass, he says, one must also study what it depends on, its competitors, and ultimately the whole aquatic environment.

## One fish, a whole lake

Forbes details the black bass's diet: fish of all the major orders, insects (water bugs, mayfly larvae), crayfish, freshwater shrimp, and a multitude of entomostracans, small crustaceans. Two links removed, the fish thus depends on almost every class of animal in the lake. Its competitors are just as numerous: all young fish feed at first almost exclusively on entomostracans.

He adds an unexpected rival, the bladderwort, a carnivorous plant, most often rootless, that fills vast stretches of the shallow lakes of northern Illinois. Ten of its bladders, taken at random from a mature plant, contain 93 animals of 28 species, 76 of them entomostracans. The plant therefore takes, he estimates, a share of the young fishes' food.

## The equilibrium

Despite enormous reproduction and enemies everywhere, each species holds from year to year within roughly constant limits of numbers. Forbes explains this through an argument. A prey must produce a surplus of individuals to feed its predator. A predator that took more than this surplus would exhaust its own food. Between these mortal enemies there is therefore a common interest. Natural selection eliminates poorly adjusted pairs of species: his reasoning operates at the level of the predator-prey pair.

Forbes concludes on the ultimate benevolence of the laws of nature, a judgment rather than a measurement.

## The shift

At the start of the same paper, Forbes distinguishes two kinds of lakes. Floodplain lakes, connected to rivers and periodically flooded, are in his view far more numerous and more important in Illinois. Their life, he writes, is particularly unstable and fluctuating: each species oscillates like a pendulum, irregularly, between a maximum and a minimum. An adjustment of numbers would eventually be established, he writes, but the flood recedes well before then. When the flood falls back, a die-off follows, prey finding themselves shut in with their predators.

The other kind is the glacial lakes of the northern part of the state, connected to neighboring watercourses by thin streams, whose level varies little from one season to the next and barely from one year to the next. Forbes sees isolation, independence, and uniformity there, and it is in these lakes that he did his sampling.

In Forbes's inventory for Illinois, the isolated lakes are the least numerous: reason to ask which lakes the microcosm applies to.

repere.texte: Ten bladders taken at random from a bladderwort in the shallow lakes of northern Illinois contained 93 animals of 28 different species, including 76 entomostracans and 8 insect larvae.
repere.source: Stephen A. Forbes, “The Lake as a Microcosm,” Bulletin of the Scientific Association (Peoria, Illinois), 1887, pp. 85–86

carte.punch: Forbes (1887) sees a lake as a closed, stable world. In the same paper, other lakes oscillate.
carte.idee: In 1887, Forbes shows that the black bass depends on almost all the life of the lake, down to a carnivorous plant that takes its food. He describes an equilibrium between predators and prey, but also floodplain lakes, more numerous, whose life oscillates.

quiz.question: What reasoning does Forbes offer to explain why predators and prey stay at stable average numbers?
choix: The season's climate sets the numbers of each species every year, independently of the others
Fishing by people living along the shore caps fish numbers and, by ricochet, those of other species
Numbers are stable only in appearance, since each flood resets them to zero before they stabilize
A predator that exceeds its prey's surplus exhausts its own food; selection weeds out the poorly matched pairs
quiz.explication: Forbes appeals to neither climate nor fishing: he derives stability from the mutual adjustment of rates of multiplication and destruction, which natural selection refines. Floods, by contrast, concern the other kind of lake in his paper, the floodplain lakes, where he describes an unstable and fluctuating life.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the bladderwort represent in Forbes's paper?
choix: A filamentous alga that clogs the gills of young fish
A rootless carnivorous plant that takes a share of the young fishes' food
A parasite that attaches to crayfish and freshwater shrimp
An introduced plant that wiped out the lake's entomostracans
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The bladderwort is a carnivorous plant, most often rootless, whose bladders contain entomostracans that young fish also eat.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Forbes, which lakes are the most numerous and most important in Illinois?
choix: The isolated glacial lakes of the northern part of the state
Artificial lakes dug for agricultural irrigation
Lakes with limestone beds in the center of the state
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Forbes says floodplain lakes are far more numerous and important, but his sampling covers the other kind, the isolated glacial lakes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before whom and when does Forbes present “The Lake as a Microcosm”?
choix: Before the American Association for the Advancement of Science, in 1895
Before the University of Illinois, on September 12, 1890
Before the Academy of Sciences in Washington, in 1872
Before the Peoria Scientific Association (Illinois), on February 25, 1887
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Forbes read his paper on February 25, 1887, before the Peoria Scientific Association in Illinois.
